name_native: 港式奶茶 / 絲襪奶茶
name_romanized: Gong sik naai caa / Si mat naai caa
origin_region: Hong Kong's cha chaan teng cafés; the leaf is a blend of several Ceylon black tea grades, sometimes with a little Chinese black or pu-erh
processing: A preparation rather than a tea: a house blend of coarse, medium and fine broken Ceylon black teas is boiled hard, poured repeatedly through a long cloth filter bag (the 'silk stocking', stained tea-brown with use) to extract and smooth it, simmered again, then mixed with evaporated milk and sugar.
harvest_season: Not a harvest: the Ceylon blends are shipped year-round and the drink is made fresh all day, every day.
appearance_dry: A dark, dust-like mix of small broken Ceylon leaf grades, from coarse bits to fine fannings.
appearance_liquor: Opaque, dark red-brown tea that turns a smooth, glossy caramel-tan once the evaporated milk is stirred in.
appearance_wet: A thick dark sludge of spent fannings in the filter bag.
taste_profile: Very strong, tannic black tea with a bitter backbone, softened into something rich, creamy and sweet by evaporated milk; thick and smooth with a long astringent finish that keeps it from being cloying.

brewing.notes: Boil 30 g of a Ceylon-based blend in a litre of water for 3–5 minutes, pour it through a cloth filter into a second pot and back again four or five times, then simmer another few minutes. Fill a cup about a third with evaporated milk, top with hot tea, sweeten to taste. Over ice it becomes the café's 'dung naai caa'.

vintage_note: No vintage. Every café guards its own blend, usually three to five Ceylon broken grades in proportions nobody will tell you, bought year-round from Hong Kong tea merchants; the same merchants sell ready-made 'milk tea blends' in bags and tins for home use, and instant 3-in-1 sachets exist for the desperate. The evaporated milk is as important as the tea and the Dutch 'Black & White' brand is the traditional one. The technique of making it was added to Hong Kong's list of intangible cultural heritage in the 2010s.
description:
Hong Kong milk tea is the drink of the cha chaan teng, the city's fast, cheap, all-day cafés: black tea brewed brutally strong, pulled through a cloth filter until it is smooth as silk, then cut with evaporated milk and sugar. It is a colonial leftover (British tea with milk) remade into something entirely Hong Kong, and locals judge a café by it the way Italians judge a bar by its espresso.

The tea is a blend of several Ceylon broken grades, coarse leaf for aroma, fine fannings for colour and strength, and each café has its own recipe. The method is the real craft: the tea is boiled, then poured through a long cloth bag on a metal ring, back and forth between two pots, which extracts the leaf fully and takes the rough edges off, and it is kept hot and strong on the stove through the day. The bag, stained brown with use, looks like a stocking, hence the nickname.

The cup is thick, strong and bitter underneath, creamy and sweet on top, with a lingering astringency that makes a second cup inevitable; evaporated milk, not fresh, gives the body, and condensed milk makes the sweeter variant called cha chow. Iced it is one of the best cold drinks in the city. The mistake at home is using a mild tea or fresh milk: the whole balance depends on an over-brewed, tannic base meeting a rich milk.

There is nothing to know about vintage, only about blends and technique. Hong Kong tea merchants sell milk-tea blends for home use; failing that, strong Ceylon fannings or a CTC breakfast tea boiled hard and strained through a cloth will get you most of the way.

Drink it with a pineapple bun or buttered toast, the classic café order, and if you want to see the tradition recognised, it was listed as part of Hong Kong's intangible cultural heritage.
